title: Interpret factors influencing agricultural enterprises and plan accordingly

lessons.title: Factors that influence a farming enterprise
lessons.html:
What is an enterprise?

An enterprise is one production activity on the farm, such as a maize land, a beef herd, a broiler house or a vegetable tunnel. Each enterprise is affected by many factors, some the farm can control and some it cannot.

Natural factors

  • Climate and weather: rainfall amount and timing, frost dates, heat, hail and drought.
  • Soil: depth, texture, fertility, drainage and slope.
  • Water: how much is available for irrigation and stock, and its quality.
  • Pests and diseases: e.g. fall armyworm in maize, ticks and tick-borne diseases in cattle.

Economic factors

  • Input prices: fertiliser, diesel, feed, electricity
  • Product prices, which often change with supply and the exchange rate
  • Interest rates on loans and overdrafts
  • Distance and transport cost to markets

Market factors

  • Who buys the product: a co-op, a fresh produce market, a supermarket, a feedlot, an abattoir
  • Quality standards and certification the buyer requires
  • Seasonal demand, e.g. higher demand for lamb over festive seasons

Social and legal factors

  • Availability and skill of labour, labour law and minimum wages
  • Safety laws such as the OHS Act 85 of 1993
  • Rules on chemicals (Act 36 of 1947), animal diseases (Act 35 of 1984) and water use (Act 36 of 1998)
  • Security, theft and community relations

Technology and management

New cultivars, irrigation systems, record systems and the skills of managers and workers all change what an enterprise can achieve.

As a supervisor, you see many of these factors first-hand: a dry spell, a pest outbreak or a labour shortage. Recognising them early and reporting them is part of planning.

lessons.title: Planning around the factors
lessons.html:
From information to a plan

Good planning means using what you know about the factors to decide what to do, when and with what resources.

Step 1: Gather information

  • Rainfall records and weather forecasts
  • Soil analysis results
  • Production records from past seasons (yields, mortalities, costs)
  • Market prices and buyer requirements
  • Labour and equipment available

Step 2: Interpret the information

Ask what the information means for the enterprise. For example, if the seasonal forecast suggests below-normal rain, a dryland maize plan may need a lower plant population or a shorter-season cultivar, as advised by the agronomist. If feed prices rise sharply, a broiler enterprise's margin shrinks, so feed conversion must be watched closely.

Step 3: Plan the activities

Draw up a simple activity plan:

ActivityWhenWhoResources
Soil samplingBefore plantingSupervisorAuger, bags, labels
PlantingAfter first good rainsTractor teamPlanter, seed, fertiliser
Scouting for pestsWeeklyScoutRecord sheet

Step 4: Allow for risk

  • Have a plan B, e.g. a replant option or extra feed reserve for drought.
  • Use insurance where the farm has it (e.g. hail cover).
  • Spread risk across enterprises and markets.

Step 5: Monitor and adjust

Compare what happens with the plan. Record rain, inputs used, work done and output. Report big differences to the manager so the plan can be changed in time.

Key points

  • Natural, economic, market, social, legal and technology factors all affect an enterprise.
  • Some factors can be controlled; others must be planned around.
  • Use records, forecasts and prices to make decisions.
  • Plan activities with timing, people and resources.
  • Build in risk plans and keep monitoring.

quiz.question: Which of these is an economic factor?

options.text: One production activity on the farm, such as a beef herd

quiz.question: If a seasonal forecast predicts below-normal rain, what might a dryland maize plan consider?

options.text: A lower plant population or shorter-season cultivar, as advised

quiz.question: What is the purpose of monitoring after the plan starts?

options.text: To avoid talking to the manager
To replace the plan with guesses
To compare actual results with the plan and adjust in time

options.text: Keeping a feed reserve for drought
